planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall in lean, well-drained montane soil; unlike most of its chaparral relatives, this High Sierra endemic naturally grows in moist forest openings and accepts a shadier garden site.

directions: Endemic to moist forest pockets in the High Sierra Nevada, this spreading evergreen shrub is one of the few California lilacs that genuinely prefers partial shade over full sun, making it a fit for a dappled woodland edge rather than open chaparral. It forms a wide, low mound of small, finely toothed leaves topped with rounded clusters of blue to lavender flowers in late spring. Once established it needs little supplemental water and resents soggy, heavy soil, so site it on a slope or raised bed with fast drainage. Avoid phosphorus fertilizer and summer irrigation around the root crown, since like other Ceanothus it fixes its own nitrogen and is prone to root rot in wet soil.

common_name: Snow Flurry Ceanothus (Profuse White California Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall in fast-draining soil; in hot inland gardens give this selection part-day or dappled shade rather than the full coastal sun the species usually tolerates, since afternoon shade keeps the display going longer.

directions: 'Snow Flurry' smothers itself in small, densely packed clusters of pure white flowers each spring, covering its glossy evergreen foliage so thickly the shrub appears dusted with snow. It grows quickly into a large specimen or informal hedge, and while it performs best along the foggy coast in full sun, it takes dappled to part-day shade well in hot inland gardens, where some afternoon relief extends bloom and keeps foliage from scorching. Prune lightly right after flowering only, since old wood on this species does not reliably resprout. Keep it on lean, well-drained soil with little summer water once established, as wet feet in heavy soil quickly leads to root rot.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in fall in average-dry, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to sun; this creeping California/Oregon native stays low enough to use as a woodland-edge groundcover.

directions: This low, suckering Oregon grape forms a creeping mat of gray-green pinnate leaves only six to twelve inches tall, making it one of the most compact Mahonia species for a dry-shade groundcover. Thick racemes of dark yellow flowers open in late spring and are followed by blue-black berries, while the foliage itself colors up with purple, red, and blue-green tones where it gets at least half a day of sun. It tolerates part shade to full sun equally well and, once established, needs little supplemental water. Site it on a dry slope or beneath open-canopy trees where larger shrubs would be too much, and avoid heavy, poorly drained soil.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in a warm, sheltered spot in sun or part shade; give this Mexican species protection from cold, drying winter winds at the cooler edge of its range.

directions: Pale mahonia carries narrower, more restrained blue-gray-green pinnate foliage than many of its relatives, giving it a softer texture in the garden. Small, pale greenish-white flowers open in long, drooping panicles from midsummer into autumn, later than most Mahonia, and ripen into blue-black berries with a white waxy bloom. It adapts to a wide range of soils and tolerates both full sun and partial shade, though it does best in humus-rich, moist-but-drained ground with shelter from harsh wind. Once rooted in, it is notably drought tolerant for the genus.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, well-drained montane soil on an open or part-shaded slope; this Klamath-Siskiyou native flowers most heavily with some direct sun but tolerates the dappled light of an open woodland planting.

directions: Found on open and wooded mountain slopes of southwest Oregon and far northern California, Piper's Oregon grape is a compact relative of the common Oregon grape, distinguished by its shorter stature and broader, more rounded leaflets on evergreen pinnate foliage. Fragrant yellow flowers cluster along the stems in spring and draw hummingbirds, ripening into waxy dark blue berries by summer. It grows naturally in part shade at the edge of conifer forest openings, though flowering is heaviest where it gets at least a few hours of direct sun. Give it sharply drained, lean soil and minimal summer water once established, since it comes from dry montane slopes.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, limestone-based soil in half sun to part shade with occasional summer water; this Mexican native comes from dry ravines in open pine forest and handles neglect once established.

directions: This Mexican barberry grows into a tall, arching shrub clothed in glossy, spineless-looking evergreen leaflets that stay attractive through all seasons. Short spikes of bright yellow flowers open as early as midwinter, followed by edible purple-blue berries with a frosted bloom. Native to dry limestone ravines in open pine forest, it thrives in half sun to part shade and tolerates both drought and poor soil once roots are established, though occasional summer water improves its appearance. Site it as an informal screen or background shrub at the edge of tree canopy rather than in deep shade, where flowering and fruiting will be sparser.
